A neuron receives signals through its dendrites, integrates them in its cell
body, then passes the result along its axon. Simple to state, this idea took
decades to establish.

::: {.illustration .illustration--droite .column-screen style="--img: url('/design/img/cajal-purkinje-1899.webp')"}
::: {.illustration-texte}
## Drawing to discover

In the late 19^th^ century, Santiago Ramón y Cajal examined nervous tissue
stained with Golgi's method and drew it by hand. His drawings showed that the
brain is made of distinct cells, neurons, that communicate by contact rather
than continuity: the origin of the neuron doctrine. He shared the 1906 Nobel
Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Camillo Golgi.

*Background image: Purkinje cells, drawing by Cajal (1899), public domain
(see the credits at the bottom of the page).*
:::
:::

## Anatomy of a multipolar neuron

Most neurons in the central nervous system are multipolar: a single axon, and
many dendrites that allow the cell to integrate a lot of information coming
from other neurons.

![Diagram of a multipolar neuron. *Image: Bruce Blaus / Blausen.com, [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/), via Wikimedia Commons.*](../../design/img/blausen-multipolar-neuron.webp){fig-alt="Annotated diagram of a multipolar neuron: cell body with nucleus, branching dendrites, a long myelinated axon and axon terminals."}
